idiom_name: for-in over Sequence (makeIterator/IteratorProtocol), plus Sequence.forEach and map/filter/reduce
implementation_notes: Swift's for-in is the enumeration message: the compiler calls makeIterator() on any Sequence and drives IteratorProtocol.next() until it returns nil, so a custom type becomes enumerable by conforming to Sequence (or, for indexable data, to Collection). The standard library's message forms carry the transforming cases - forEach for side effects, map/compactMap/filter/reduce for results, lazy for deferred sequences - and enumerated()/zip() supply the index or a partner sequence. Index loops (for i in 0..<xs.count) belong to algorithms that address positions, since subscripting is O(1) only for RandomAccessCollection.
pitfalls: forEach cannot break or continue and returns Void; a walk that stops early must use for-in, first(where:) or contains(where:).

Conforming a type to Sequence with an iterator that is itself (a single-pass IteratorProtocol wrapper) makes a second for-in over the same value yield nothing; conform to Collection or return a fresh iterator when re-iteration is expected.

Mutating a value-type collection inside for-in iterates the loop's own copy, so the changes are invisible during the walk; gather them and apply afterwards, while reference-type collections can trap or misbehave when resized mid-iteration.
